name: Point Class Hierarchy (Case 2)
description: Suppose we have a class Point and we want to extend it to produce class Point3D. The class Point has two data members, x and y that represent the point's integer coordinates in the two-dimensional space. A Point3D has three data members, x, y, and z that represent the point's integer coordinates in the three-dimensional space. For each class, write the class declaration, the constructor, the toString method, and a method to move (translate) the point, i.e., shift the point's location by the specified amount.\n\nThe class InheritancePointTester2 tests these classes and their methods.

comments.content: This statement creates a Point object with the specified x and y coordinate. Note that we create this object by using the new keyword and writing its initial values in parentheses (x,y). The variable p holds a reference to the Point object.
Note that we can create a Point object with the specified x and y values only when we have a constructor in the class Point that accepts these parameters.

This statement invokes the method translate of p. The translate method receives two parameters. The first parameter specifies how much we want to shift the x-coordinate of the point. The second parameter specifies how much we want to shift the y-coordinate of the point.

When we pass a Point object to a print or println method (or when we concatenate an object to a character string), the toString method of that object gets called automatically. Therefore, this statement prints the string that is returned from invoking the toString method of the class Point. The printed text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.

This statement creates a Point3D object with the specified x, y, and z coordinate. Note that we create this object by using the new keyword and writing its initial values in parentheses (x,y,z). The variable p3d holds a reference to the Point3D object.
Note that we can create a Point3D object with the specified x, y, and z values only when we have a constructor in the class Point3D that accepts these parameters.

This statement invokes the method translate of p3d. The translate method receives three parameters. The first parameter specifies how much we want to shift the x-coordinate of the point, the second parameter specifies how much we want to shift the y-coordinate of the point, and the third parameter specifies how much we want to shift the z-coordinate of the point.

When we pass a Point3D object to a print or println method (or when we concatenate an object to a character string), the toString method of that object gets called automatically. Therefore, this statement prints the string that is returned from invoking the toString method of the class Point3D. The printed text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.
The class Point provides some functionality for a Point with xy-coordinates.

Every object of the Point1 class will have its own x-coordinate. Therefore, we need to declare an instance variable for the class to store the x-coordinate of the point. We declare it as integer because we want to have integer coordinates for the point.

Note that an instance variable is a variable defined in a class, for which each instantiated object of the class has a separate copy, or instance.

Note that the instance variables should be declared as private to restrict the direct access or change from outside the class. In this way, no unexpected modification of the object data is possible.

We could access/change the private instance variables of the class only through the getters/setters methods of the class.

Every object of the Point1 class will have its own y-coordinate. Therefore, we need to declare an instance variable for the class to store the y-coordinate of the point. We declare it as integer because we want to have integer coordinates for the point.

Note that an instance variable is a variable defined in a class, for which each instantiated object of the class has a separate copy, or instance.

Note that the instance variables should be declared as private to restrict the direct access or change from outside the class. In this way, no unexpected modification of the object data is possible.

We could access/change the private instance variables of the class only through the getters/setters methods of the class.
To create a point with the specified xy-coordinate, we need to have a constructor of the class Point that accepts initial values for Point's x-coordinate and y-coordinate.

Note that the constructor definition starts with the access specifier (public), name of the constructor (always the same as the name of the class) and the list of parameters (to initialize the instance fields of newly created objects). Unlike methods, constructors do not have a return type.

This statement sets instance variable x to the first parameter value (x). Note that the this reference is used to distinguish the parameter of the constructor from its corresponding instance variable with the same name.

This statement sets instance variable y to the second parameter value (y). Note that the this reference is used to distinguish the parameter of the constructor from its corresponding instance variable with the same name.

This method shifts the coordinates by a specific delta-x (dx) and delta-y (dy), which are passed as parameters. We define this method as public to provide access to this method from outside of the class. Also, we define its return type as void, as it does not return any value.

Note that both of the parameters are declared as integers because the point has integer coordinates.
To shift the x-coordinate of the point, we need to add dx to the value of the x-coordinate of the point.

The += operator adds the value on the right-hand side of the assignment operator (i.e., value of variable dx) to the current value of the variable on the left-hand side (i.e., value of the instance variable x) and the result is stored in the instance variable x. Thus, this statement is equivalent to the statement x = x + dx.
To shift the y-coordinate of the point, we need to add dy to the value of the y-coordinate of the point.

The += operator adds the value on the right-hand side of the assignment operator (i.e., value of variable dy) to the current value of the variable on the left-hand side (i.e., value of the instance variable y) and the result is stored in the instance variable y. Thus, this statement is equivalent to the statement y = y + dy.

This method returns a String representation of the Point object. We define this method as public to provide access to this method from outside of the class. Also, we define its return type as String, as it returns a description of the Point instance that is a String.
Note that this method is called automatically when we pass a Point object to a print or println method (or when we concatenate an object to a character string).

This method returns the x-coordinate of the point. We define this method as public to provide access to this method from outside of the class. Also, we define its return type as int, as it returns the x-coordinate of the point which is an integer.

Note that the instance variable x is private; thus, it cannot be directly accessed from outside the class. It can be accessed from outside the class only through this getter method.

This method returns the y-coordinate of the point. We define this method as public to provide access to this method from outside of the class. Also, we define its return type as int, as it returns the y-coordinate of the point which is an integer.

Note that the instance variable y is private; thus, it cannot be directly accessed from outside the class. It can be accessed from outside the class only through this method.

The class Point3D extends the Point to model the Point3D objects. By extending Point, Point3D inherits all the member data (instance variable) and methods that belong to Point class, provided that the data/method is declared with either a public or protected access modifier.

Every object of the class Point3D will have its own xyz-coordinates. The x and y variables is indirectly available in class Point3D because Point3D inherited the public accessor method getX() and getY() from Point. Therefore, we only need to declare an instance variable for the class to store the z-coordinate of the 3D point. We declare the z-coordinate as integer because we want to have integer coordinates for the point.

Note that an instance variable is a variable defined in a class, for which each instantiated object of the class has a separate copy, or instance.

Note that the instance variables should be declared as private to restrict the direct access or change from outside the class. In this way, no unexpected modification of the object data is possible.

We could access/change the private instance variables of the class only through the getters/setters methods of the class.
To create a 3d point with the specified x, y, and z coordinates, we need to have a constructor of the class Point3D that accepts initial value for the point's x, y, and z.

Note that the constructor definition starts with the access specifier (public), name of the constructor (always the same as the name of the class) and the list of parameters (to initialize the instance fields of newly created objects). Unlike methods, constructors do not have a return type.

Point3D is a subclass of class Point. Therefore; when we want to create a Point3D object, we need to first invoke the constructor of the class Point that creates a Point object with the specified xy-coordinate. The call to constructor of the super class MUST be made in the first line of the subclass, otherwise we will get a compile error.

If a constructor does not explicitly invoke a superclass constructor, the Java compiler automatically inserts a call to the no-argument constructor of the superclass. However, if the super class does not have a no-argument constructor (as in the class Point), we will get an error.

This statement sets instance variable z to the value of the third parameter of the constructor (z). Note that the this reference is used to distinguish the parameter of the constructor from its corresponding instance variable with the same name.

This method shifts the coordinates by a specific delta-x (dx), delta-y (dy) and delta-z (dz), which are passed as parameters. We define this method as public to provide access to this method from outside of the class. Also, we define its return type as void, as it does not return any value.

Note that the parameters are declared as integers because the point has integer coordinates.
This statement invokes the method translate of the superclass to move the x-coordinate and y-coordinate of the point with the specified amount.
To shift the z-coordinate of the point, we need to add dz to the value of the z-coordinate of the point.

The += operator adds the value on the right-hand side of the assignment operator (i.e., value of variable dz) to the current value of the variable on the left-hand side (i.e., value of the instance variable z) and the result is stored in the instance variable z. Thus, this statement is equivalent to the statement z = z + dz.

This method returns the z-coordinate of the point. We define this method as public to provide access to this method from outside of the class. Also, we define its return type as int, as it returns the z-coordinate of the point which is an integer.

Note that the instance variable z is private; thus, it cannot be directly accessed from outside the class. It can be accessed from outside the class only through this method.

Since the class Point3D includes the method "toString()", the toString() method in Point is overridden in Point3D. We override the toString method of the class Point to return the String representation of the Point3D object that not only shows the xy-coordinate but also show's the z-coordinate of the 3D point. We get this string by invoking getX and getY method of the Point's class and concatenating that with the Point3D z-coordinate.

We define this method as public to provide access to this method from outside of the class. Also, we define its return type as String, as it returns a description of the Point3D instance that is a String.
Note that this method is called automatically when we pass a Point3D's object to a print or println method (or when we concatenate an object to a character string).

This statement concatenates the string returned from invoking the getX and getY method of the superclass with the given strings and value of instance variable z.
super.getX() invoke the getX method of the superclass (Point).
super.getY() invoke the getY method of the superclass (Point).
